dossiers.title: Evil, Suffering, and Theodicy
dossiers.question: How should the Way understand suffering, moral evil, natural evil, and the apparent tension between suffering and claims about divine goodness or power?
witnesses: Hebrew Bible laments, Job, prophetic protest, and wisdom traditions
Jesus traditions concerning suffering, compassion, healing, and unjust death
Qur'anic traditions of trial, patience, justice, mercy, and accountability
Buddhist analysis of dukkha and its conditions
Philosophical arguments from evil and major theodicy families
findings: Established
Human suffering is real, morally urgent, unevenly distributed, and cannot responsibly be reduced to a single cause.
Established
The existence and intensity of suffering pose a serious evidential challenge to some forms of all-powerful, all-knowing, perfectly good theism. [S1-S2]
Well-supported

Religious traditions respond differently: protest/lament, free-will accounts, soul-making, karma/rebirth, eschatological repair, mystery, compassion, and liberation all occur, but each has significant interpretive and philosophical difficulties.
Established ethical rule

No House of Prayer may presume that illness, disability, disaster, abuse, infertility, poverty, bereavement, or other suffering is divine punishment, karmic desert, weak faith, or spiritual failure without extraordinary evidence.
Established ethical rule

A theological explanation must never be used to silence lament, block medical or legal help, pressure forgiveness, excuse an abuser, or tell a victim that suffering was necessary for another person's spiritual growth.
open: Whether God is omnipotent/omniscient/perfectly good in classical terms
Whether some suffering has divinely intended purposes
Whether there is karmic moral causation across lives
Whether final eschatological repair can justify or redeem horrendous suffering
Whether some forms of evil count as positive evidence against particular God-concepts
change: A coherent model that explains severe apparently gratuitous suffering without moral distortion
Reliable evidence of moral causation beyond ordinary natural/social mechanisms
Stronger arguments regarding divine attributes, freedom, providence, or cosmic justice
dossiers.baseline: The Way may teach compassion, lament, resistance to preventable harm, care for sufferers, and epistemic restraint. It must not teach that all suffering is deserved or divinely scripted.

dossiers.title: Salvation, Liberation, Healing, and Awakening
dossiers.question: What, if anything, is the basic human problem and what constitutes its healing, liberation, reconciliation, awakening, or completion?
witnesses: Jewish themes of covenant faithfulness, repentance, deliverance, justice, and restoration
Christian themes of reconciliation, grace, participation in divine life, forgiveness, resurrection, and salvation
Islamic themes of submission to God, mercy, repentance, righteous action, judgment, and felicity
Buddhist liberation from suffering, craving, ignorance, and cyclical becoming
Hindu, Jain, mystical, and philosophical liberation traditions
findings: Established
"Salvation" is a useful comparative category but originated in particular theological contexts and can distort other traditions if treated as a universal equivalent. [S3]
Established
Religions diagnose the human condition differently; therefore their proposed ends are not simply interchangeable.
Well-supported

Across traditions there is recurring concern with transformation from alienation, ignorance, wrongdoing, bondage, suffering, disorder, or estrangement toward wholeness, reconciliation, awakening, liberation, holiness, or right relationship.
Established ethical rule

No leader or institution may sell, guarantee, withhold, or threaten a person's ultimate spiritual destiny in exchange for money, loyalty, sexual access, silence, labor, housing, votes, or continued membership.
open: Whether there is one universal human spiritual problem
Whether reconciliation with God, awakening, liberation, or moral transformation is the deepest end
Whether multiple religious paths are genuinely salvific/liberative
Whether salvation is possible after death
Whether final reconciliation is universal, conditional, or otherwise structured
change: Better comparative analysis showing equivalence or incompatibility among claimed ends
Historical and experiential evidence concerning transformative practices
Stronger metaphysical account of personhood, God, consciousness, and death
dossiers.baseline: The Way may speak provisionally of healing, liberation, reconciliation, awakening, and wholeness, while refusing to collapse them into one metaphysical claim before evidence warrants it.

dossiers.title: Death, Resurrection, Rebirth, and Afterlife
dossiers.question: What happens at death, if anything, and what kinds of postmortem continuity are coherent or evidenced?
witnesses: Jewish developments from Sheol traditions to resurrection and later eschatologies
Christian resurrection, judgment, heaven/hell, purgation, and universalist traditions
Islamic resurrection, judgment, paradise, hell, mercy, and disputed duration questions
Buddhist and Hindu rebirth traditions and liberation from cycles of becoming
Philosophical arguments concerning dualism, materialism, personal identity, resurrection, reincarnation, and consciousness
findings: Established
Human cultures and religious traditions contain multiple incompatible models of postmortem existence. [S4]
Established
Bodily resurrection, disembodied survival, reincarnation/rebirth, universal reconciliation, eternal separation, annihilation, and cessation are conceptually distinct proposals, not synonyms.
Established
The philosophical possibility of an afterlife depends heavily on theories of mind, personal identity, and continuity; no single model is established merely by widespread belief. [S4]
Established
Christian traditions themselves contain substantial diversity regarding heaven, hell, punishment, freedom, and universal reconciliation. [S5]
Established pastoral rule
Funerals and memorials must distinguish memory, hope, inherited tradition, and metaphysical certainty. No officiant may claim knowledge of a deceased person's final destiny without warrant.
open: Whether consciousness survives biological death
Whether resurrection occurs and what preserves personal identity
Whether rebirth occurs and how identity persists without a permanent self
Whether judgment is personal, cosmic, restorative, punitive, or metaphorical
Whether all persons are ultimately reconciled/liberated
change: Strong reproducible evidence of postmortem consciousness or verified past-life memory
A compelling theory of personal identity across death
Stronger historical evidence for specific resurrection/rebirth claims
A more coherent account of divine justice and universal destiny
dossiers.baseline: The Way adopts hope without fabrication: death is certain; grief is real; ultimate destiny remains an open question. Memorial practice may express hope while naming uncertainty.

dossiers.title: Sexuality, Marriage, Family, and Intimate Ethics
dossiers.question: What ethical principles should govern sexuality, marriage, partnership, family, celibacy, parenting, and intimate power?
witnesses: Jewish, Christian, and Islamic marriage/family law and theology in diverse historical forms
Buddhist monastic and lay sexual ethics
Contemporary family structures and empirical research on religion and family
Modern theological debates concerning gender, sexuality, marriage, celibacy, divorce, and same-sex relationships
findings: Established
Religious teachings on sexuality and family vary substantially across traditions and within traditions over time. [S6-S7]
Established

Marriage has served multiple functions historically: kinship, property, procreation, companionship, covenant, sacrament, social order, and legal status; one function should not be projected backward as the only universal meaning.
Established ethical rule
Valid intimate relationships require capacity, meaningful consent, freedom from coercion, truthfulness about commitments, and protection from exploitation.
Established ethical rule
Sexual access can never be a privilege of spiritual office. Pastoral, ministerial, therapeutic-like, residential, employment, or dependency power requires heightened boundaries.
Established ethical rule
Children cannot consent to sexual activity with adults; safeguarding supersedes claims of custom, revelation, marriage arrangement, spiritual status, or family authority.
Well-supported

Stable care, equitable responsibility, nonviolence, honesty, fidelity to freely undertaken commitments, and protection of dependents are strong cross-context ethical goods even where family forms differ.
open: Whether marriage should become a sacrament/rite of the Way
The Way's theology of sex difference, gender, celibacy, contraception, divorce/remarriage, and same-sex unions
Whether plural marriage can ever meet the Way's equality/noncoercion standards
How dual-religion/interfaith marriages should be recognized ritually
The relationship between procreation and marriage
change: Careful textual/historical research by tradition
Evidence concerning flourishing, harm, coercion, children, dependency, and family stability
Coherent theological account of body, personhood, covenant, and sexuality
dossiers.baseline: Before settling disputed sexual theology, the Way can already require consent, non-exploitation, honesty, care, safeguarding, and equality before institutional processes. No Companion is required to marry, reproduce, remain married, or disclose intimate information to retain spiritual standing.

dossiers.title: Violence, Nonviolence, Defense, and Peace
dossiers.question: Does the Way require pacifism, permit defensive force, or recognize justifiable violence under limited conditions?
witnesses: Hebrew Bible traditions ranging from warfare to prophetic peace visions
Jesus traditions concerning enemy-love, peacemaking, nonretaliation, and protection of the vulnerable
Islamic texts and jurisprudential traditions on conflict, restraint, defense, peace, and no compulsion
Buddhist and Jain non-harming traditions
Christian pacifist and just-war traditions; modern philosophical pacifism
findings: Established
Pacifism itself contains multiple positions, from absolute nonviolence to narrower opposition to war. [S8]
Established
Religious traditions contain both peace-making resources and texts/traditions used to justify force; selective quotation can conceal this internal diversity.
Established institutional rule

No founder, minister, elder, council, or House of Prayer may declare a private war, authorize vigilantism, command violence, create armed religious enforcement, or claim revelatory exemption from civil law.
Established ethical rule
Peace obtained by coercive domination is not sufficient merely because overt conflict has stopped; justice and protection of vulnerable persons matter. [S8]
Well-supported
The Way should begin with a strong presumption for nonviolent prevention, de-escalation, reconciliation where safe, restorative practices, and peacebuilding.
open: Whether absolute pacifism is ultimately required
Whether proportionate force in immediate defense of self or others is morally permissible
Whether participation in military or police service is compatible with the Way
How to evaluate state warfare, humanitarian intervention, and resistance to tyranny
change: A stronger theological account of enemy-love, justice, state authority, and protection obligations
Historical evidence about outcomes of violent and nonviolent resistance
Moral analysis of extreme rescue and defense cases
dossiers.baseline: The Way adopts a presumption toward nonviolence and peacemaking but does not yet declare absolute pacifism. Religious authority never grants an independent license to harm.

dossiers.title: Rites, Sacraments, Symbols, and Sacred Mediation
dossiers.question: What can rites do, and do any rites mediate divine grace or spiritual reality beyond their communal, ethical, and psychological functions?
witnesses: Jewish ritual, covenantal, purity, festival, and lifecycle practices
Christian sacramental, ordinance, baptismal, eucharistic, marriage, healing, and funerary traditions
Islamic prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, almsgiving, recitation, and lifecycle practice
Buddhist refuge, precepts, ordination, meditation, offering, funeral, and merit practices
Anthropological and historical study of ritual and rites of passage
findings: Established
Rites create and transmit meaning, memory, identity, commitment, and communal transition even before metaphysical efficacy is established.
Established
Religions differ sharply over whether rites symbolize grace, convey grace, enact covenant, transform status, purify, generate merit, or function principally as communal practice.
Established institutional rule
No rite may erase consent, create ownership of a person, bypass safeguarding, transfer property automatically, impose an irreversible child commitment, or authorize sexual/financial access.
Established
A community can responsibly practice provisional rites while clearly labeling what is symbolic, hoped, inherited, or doctrinally unresolved.
open: Whether any rite objectively mediates divine grace
Whether the Way should have baptism-like initiation, eucharistic/sacramental meal, marriage sacrament, anointing, confession, or funerary sacrament
Whether physical substances/gestures can carry objective sacred status
Which rites require commissioned ministers and which belong to all Companions
change: Historical-theological evidence concerning source traditions
Longitudinal experience of the Way's provisional rites
A developed theology of God, embodiment, community, and mediation
dossiers.baseline: Rites may be used now as truthful communal practices whose claimed efficacy is no stronger than the evidence and theology supporting them.

dossiers.title: Ordination, Ministry, Charisma, and Religious Office
dossiers.question: Should the Way recognize an ordained clergy, and if so what is conferred by ordination?
witnesses: Israelite priestly, prophetic, scribal, and elder roles
Early Christian apostles, overseers, elders, deacons, teachers, and later ordination traditions
Islamic scholars, imams, jurists, Sufi guides, and non-sacramental leadership patterns
Buddhist and Jain monastic ordination systems
Sikh, Quaker, and other traditions with differing clergy/laity structures
findings: Established
Ordination is not one universal religious institution; communities construct religious office differently and encode different theologies in rites. [S9-S10]
Established
Historical charisma and institutional office are distinguishable; claims of spiritual gifting do not automatically create legal, financial, disciplinary, or safeguarding authority.
Established institutional rule
The Way's current commissioning system is sufficient to authorize defined ministry functions without asserting ontological superiority.
Established institutional rule

No ordination or commissioning may grant immunity, doctrinal infallibility, founder-like succession, sexual access, control over another adult's conscience, or unilateral authority over money/property.
open: Whether ordination should eventually be adopted in addition to commissioning
Whether ordination changes status sacramentally/ontologically or only authorizes function
Whether ministry should be time-limited, renewable, lifelong, or mixed by role
Which ministries require formal credentialing
change: Developed theology of sacred mediation and vocation
Practical experience across multiple Houses
Comparative study of clericalization, abuse risks, and durable ministry formation
dossiers.baseline: Commissioning remains the operative authorization. Ordination stays reserved until theology requires something commissioning cannot truthfully express.

dossiers.title: Sacred Time, Weekly Rhythm, Calendar, Fasting, and Festivals
dossiers.question: How should the Way organize recurring sacred time without fabricating ancient authority or prematurely freezing a calendar?
witnesses: Jewish Sabbath and festival cycles
Christian weekly and annual liturgical calendars
Islamic daily prayer, Friday gathering, lunar calendar, Ramadan, pilgrimage seasons, and feasts
Buddhist lunar observances, Vesak and regional festival cycles
Seasonal, agricultural, commemorative, penitential, and pilgrimage calendars across traditions
findings: Established
Religious calendars do more than mark dates: recurring ritual time shapes memory, identity, practice, generosity, repentance, and community. [S11-S13,S19-S20]
Established
The seven-day sacred rhythm has enormous historical influence, but traditions locate sacred weekly gathering differently. [S12]
Established
Festivals often combine remembered events, natural cycles, communal meals, prayer, generosity, fasting, pilgrimage, and teaching rather than serving one function only.
Established ethical rule
Fasting and vigils must include health, age, pregnancy, disability, medication, eating-disorder, labor, and other exemptions; spiritual status must never depend on unsafe observance.
open: Which day or days should carry primary weekly communal significance
Whether the Way adopts a distinctive calendar or uses civil/local calendars with an observance overlay
Which historical events deserve annual remembrance
Whether fasting becomes normative, optional, seasonal, or remains individual
How inherited Jewish, Christian, Islamic, Buddhist, and other holy days should be observed by Companions
change: Actual practice and needs of Houses of Prayer
Theology of creation, revelation, historical memory, and rest
Calendar research and global cultural/astronomical practicality
dossiers.baseline: Adopt recurring sacred rhythm before adopting a total calendar: regular prayer, weekly communal gathering/rest rhythm, periodic service and self-examination, and annual remembrance may develop experimentally with transparent revision.

dossiers.title: Interreligious Identity, Dialogue, Conversion, and Dual Belonging
dossiers.question: How should the Way relate to other religions and to Companions who retain, revise, or relinquish prior religious identities?
witnesses: Abrahamic claims of continuity, fulfillment, supersession, covenant, prophecy, and finality
Buddhist transmission and adaptation across cultures
Sikh and Bahá'í engagements with religious plurality
Modern interreligious dialogue principles
Historical conversion movements and coercive/voluntary conversion patterns
findings: Established
Religions make genuinely different and sometimes contradictory truth claims; respectful dialogue does not require pretending all claims are identical. [S14,S17]
Established
Religious conversion historically ranges from highly voluntary to socially or politically coerced; volition therefore requires explicit protection. [S16]
Established ethical rule

The Way prohibits compelled conversion and institutional penalties for declining conversion. The Qur'anic no-compulsion witness is one important historical source among others for this principle. [S15]
Established

Source traditions must be represented in their own terms before the Way evaluates them. The Way should not strip-mine traditions for attractive practices while ignoring context, ownership, history, or living communities.
Established institutional rule
Companions may maintain ordinary family, friendship, study, worship-visiting, and dialogue relationships outside the Way; leaders may not require social isolation.
open: Whether formal dual religious belonging is coherent for every combination of traditions
Whether the Way eventually understands itself as a new religion, reform movement, meta-tradition, fellowship, or another category
Whether some source traditions are uniquely revelatory or salvifically normative
How to handle incompatible initiation vows or exclusive doctrinal commitments
change: Long-term lived experience of Companions with multiple inheritances
Dialogue with representatives and scholars of source traditions
Further research on truth, revelation, salvation/liberation, and religious identity
dossiers.baseline: The Way practices neither "all religions are the same" nor "all others are false." It adopts disciplined hospitality: learn accurately, preserve disagreement, protect conscience, cooperate in good work, and test claims without coercion.

baseline: Do not presume suffering is deserved, divinely inflicted, karmically deserved, or evidence of weak faith; protect lament, care, treatment, and justice.
No single theodicy is adopted. Proposed explanations must face horrendous suffering and may not be used to silence victims.
Use healing, liberation, reconciliation, awakening, wholeness, and right relationship as comparative/working terms without declaring them metaphysically identical.
No current teaching that only Companions can be saved/liberated; no leader may claim knowledge of another person's ultimate destiny.
No settled teaching yet on resurrection, heaven/hell, rebirth, annihilation, or postmortem consciousness.
Speak truthfully: honor the dead, support mourners, distinguish hope from certainty, and never exploit grief.
Require capacity, meaningful consent, non-exploitation, honesty, safeguarding, and faithful responsibility to freely undertaken commitments and dependents.
Marriage/covenant blessing remains reserved pending research on sacramentality, gender/sex, divorce, remarriage, same-sex unions, celibacy, and family plurality.
Strong presumption toward nonviolence, peacemaking, de-escalation, and protection of vulnerable persons; absolute pacifism remains open.
No House, minister, founder, elder, or council can authorize vigilantism, holy war, coercive enforcement, or revelatory exemption from law.
Rites may express commitment, memory, transition, healing, and community; metaphysical efficacy must be stated only at the confidence warranted.
Commissioning authorizes defined functions and limits; it creates no sacred caste or immunity.
Do not adopt until theology requires a claim beyond functional commissioning.
Develop a recurring weekly/seasonal rhythm experimentally before constitutionalizing a comprehensive calendar.
Optional/experimental only, with broad health and conscience exemptions until a theology and safety standard are adopted.
Represent source traditions accurately; dialogue does not require erasing difference; no compelled conversion or social isolation.
Permitted for exploration/participation; formal doctrinal coherence varies by traditions and remains under study.
